## Discussion

### Factors Associated with BMI
Ultimately, our multiple linear regression model for predicting log(BMI) identifies several statistically significant predictors, but its overall explanatory power is rather modest ($R^2$ = 0.141) (@tbl-mlr-stat). This suggests that while the model captures some meaningful relationships, a large portion of the variability in BMI may not be explained by the predictors included here, suggesting that additional behavioral or environmental factors may also play a role. The model indicates that physical activity and general health status have the strongest associations with BMI. Individuals who report engaging in physical activity tend to have lower BMI, while those reporting poorer general health tend to have higher BMI. A clear gradient is observed across health categories, where individuals with excellent health have lower BMI and those with fair or poor health have higher BMI. These findings are consistent with expected relationships between lifestyle behaviors and body weight. Other variables, such as smoking and age, were also statistically significant but had relatively small effect sizes. This suggests that while smoking and age are associated with BMI, they may not be a practically important predictor, especially given the large sample size.

The model also produced results that differ slightly from the descriptive analysis. While individuals aged 35–54 showed higher BMI compared to younger adults, there was no significant difference for individuals aged 55 and older after adjusting for other variables. This suggests that age may not remain a significant independent predictor once other health and behavioral factors are taken into account. 

For the most part, the model supports the expectation that behavioral and health-related factors are associated with BMI. However, there are also a few limitations to consider when interpreting these results. The data are self-reported, which introduces the possibility of reporting bias in measures such as physical activity and general health. In addition, the cross-sectional nature of the dataset limits the ability to draw causal conclusions, as these relationships reflect associations at a single point in time. Finally, while BIC-based model selection provides a structured way to choose predictors, it may exclude variables that are still relevant but do not substantially improve model fit.


### Predicting Heart Attack
Overall, our logistic regression model for predicting the log-odds of heart disease displays much higher classification performance than random (AUC = 0.83 for the ROC) and exhibits high sensitivity and specificity for predicting whether an individual will experience heart attack (@fig-roc). The model posits that being over 55 years of age has the greatest impact on risk for heart attack, followed by having had a stroke or being between 35-54 years old (@fig-log-reg-coefficients). On the other hand, the model claims that generally having excellent and good health are the largest contributors to decreasing risk of heart disease, followed by being male or Asian (@fig-log-reg-coefficients). For the most part, the model confirmed our expectations that pre-existing health conditions (stroke, kidney disease, diabetes, smoking, skin cancer, difficulty walking, asthma, poor health) would predispose someone to heart disease. These health complications become more common with age due to general effects of aging on human biology and increased opportunity to be exposed to unhealthy conditions, which would explain the strong effect of older age on heart disease risk. However, contrary to these findings, the model forwarded that consuming alcohol decreases the odds of heart disease (@fig-log-reg-coefficients). **INCLUDE EXPLANATION**.

The model also predicted unexpected results for the influence of demographic factors on heart attack risk. Notably, it would predict that White individuals would be at greatest risk for heart disease compared to Hispanic, Black, and Asian individuals. A possible explanation for this could be bias in the data set due to different access to health care and formal diagnosis. For instance, White individuals may more regularly attend hospital check-ups and thus may have a higher rate of heart disease diagnosis.
